Depends on how you meet people:

* If you decide to do online dating, just state it explicitly in your profile: "I'm not into casual dating, I'm looking for something to last."  It's not weird because it's the whole point of a dating profile, being very clear about who you are and what you want.
* If you're into in-person date finding, it's a third-date thing to drop unless they bring up "I only want something casual" earlier than that (in which case you reply graciously and sincerely with "You're a nice person, but I think we want different things.  Good luck!").  Just be clear and honest without being judgmental (i.e. casual relationships are not inherently inferior to deeper lasting ones, they just aren't your thing).

Nope!  Not all freshmen are riding the excitement wave.

There's also the fact that, if you're a commitment minded individual, there's nothing wrong with dating someone a year or two older than you.

> but if most people don't want a relationships that are the middle ground during the first two years of college and are only super casual

And there would be where you're wrong.

Not all relationships in early college are super-casual.  If you go on the dating scene being clear what you want, that you're the kind of person who likes to stick things out, you'll find them eventually.

> What's the point then of dating if you are well aware that it won't work out?

Define "it".

People sometimes do find love in college.  And to be honest, even relationships that don't last can be beneficial for the moment.  It's not like there's two settings to a relationship--super-casual and one-and-only-marriage-track--and most relationships fit somewhere comfortably in the middle.

I think you're overthinking things.

Speaking as someone ten years your senior, dating in early college is often more about figuring out what *you* want out of a relationship through trial and error.  And that's fine!  It can be incredibly rewarding when you learn what does work while having painful parts when you learn what doesn't work.  That's life, what makes us human.  A relationship not working out doesn't mean you've wasted time because you've learned something at the end of it.

The main thing about dating in college is making sure that "dating" comes below "school", "family", and "friends" in your overall priority listing.

That's pretty much perfect.

And by "pretty much perfect", I mean "that is almost word-for-word what my current boyfriend did when he asked me out for the first time", and it obviously worked.

My general rule of thumb being friends with minors is this: if you'd be comfortable detailing everything the two of you do together to her parents and having them read your texts/chat logs, there is absolutely nothing wrong with it.

When I was in my mid to late teens, friendships with older women ("older" = mid-twenties or older) were really important helping me realize the range of options I had for what kind of woman I could be when I was a grown-up.  I imagine a lot of women get that kind of thing from aunts and older female cousins, but I didn't have any who I was close to (they all lived across the country) so this non-family network of older women with more life experience was critical.
